MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
Happy to help, and being slightly terrified is a sensible starting point: it makes people careful.

## What "lippage" means

**Lippage** is when the edge of one tile sits higher than the edge of the tile next to it, so the surface has a small step instead of being flush. You can feel it with your foot or fingertips. Low light across the floor shows it up, it catches socks, and raised edges can chip.

It usually comes from:
- an uneven floor underneath,
- uneven adhesive, or
- the tiles themselves. Long tiles like 60 cm ones are often very slightly curved, a little higher in the middle.

The cures are a flat base, full adhesive coverage, and levelling clips (see the tips below).

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for a **mid-grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. It blends in, and it won't show dirt the way white or very pale grout does. Floor grout always darkens with foot traffic, so a light grout is the one that looks dirty within a month.

A stain-resistant grout, or sealing a standard cement-based grout once it has cured, will also help it stay clean.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Before.** Tile the whole floor, including under where the toilet will sit, then fit the toilet on top. That's far easier than cutting tiles around the base of the toilet. It gives a cleaner, more watertight finish, and you won't have a gap to deal with if the toilet is ever replaced. You'll only need to cut one hole for the waste pipe.

One check: the new floor will be about 1 cm higher, so make sure the toilet's waste connector still lines up.

## How many boxes?

**Buy 4 boxes.** The working:

| Step | Figure |
|---|---|
| Floor area | 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²** |
| One tile | 0.3 × 0.6 = **0.18 m²** |
| Tiles to cover the floor | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = **24 tiles** |
| Plus 10% | 26.4, so **27 tiles** |
| Boxes of 8 | 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **4 boxes (32 tiles)** |

Three boxes would give exactly 24 tiles with nothing to spare, so that isn't enough.

Four boxes leaves about 8 spare tiles. That's more than 10%, but it's useful:
- You'll need cuts at the edges anyway, because grout lines add a little width.
- First-timers break a tile or two.
- Keeping 2–3 spare tiles means you can repair a cracked tile years later with an exact match.

When buying, check that all boxes have the **same batch or shade number** on the label. The colour can vary slightly between batches.

## Message for the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a quick heads-up: we're tiling our bathroom floor on Saturday, so there'll be some noise from cutting tiles in the morning, roughly 9am to 12pm. We'll keep it to that window as best we can.
>
> Thank you for being so patient with the skip on the drive these past two weeks. It should be gone very soon. If anything's a problem, just knock.
>
> Thanks again,
> [Your names]

Adjust the times and the skip line to match your actual plans.

## Three tips for a first floor

1. **Prepare the base before anything else.** The floor underneath must be solid, clean and flat. Lay a long spirit level or straight edge across it in several directions. Dips or humps of more than a few millimetres will show up as lippage. Fix them first with self-levelling compound or by sanding high spots. A wooden floor needs a tile backer board or suitable plywood screwed down over it, because tiles laid straight onto floorboards crack.

2. **Lay the tiles out dry before you mix any adhesive.** Arrange them on the floor without adhesive to plan where the cuts will fall:
   - Aim for even cuts at opposite walls, not a thin sliver along one side, especially at the doorway where it shows most.
   - If you're staggering the tiles like brickwork, offset each row by a **third** of a tile, not half. With 60 cm tiles that's 20 cm, and it reduces lippage from the slight bow.
   - Plan to finish at the door so you don't tile yourself into a corner.

3. **Get full adhesive contact and check as you go.**
   - Use the notched trowel size the adhesive bag recommends.
   - Also spread a thin layer on the back of each tile ("back-buttering").
   - Press each tile down with a slight twist.
   - Lift one of the first tiles to check the back is fully covered.
   - Levelling clips are cheap and make flush edges much easier for a beginner.
   - Mix adhesive in small batches so it doesn't start setting before you've used it.

The videos do make it look quick. Professionals have the same steps; they're just faster at them. Go slowly, check often, and it will come out well.
